opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. You know, I think people sometimes misread me as a doomer, and it's actually the opposite. I'm an optimist at heart. When I look up at the night sky as a physicist, I see this enormous universe that has mostly been dead and unconscious for billions of years, and then life arose here and became aware of itself. Intelligence is what lets life flourish, and AI could help that flourishing spread far beyond anything we've imagined: curing diseases, ending poverty, helping life thrive for billions of years rather than just until the next asteroid or the next self-inflicted catastrophe.

So my optimism is precisely *why* I care so much about getting this right. If I thought the future was hopeless anyway, why bother? It's because the upside is so spectacular that it would be such a tragedy to blow it through hubris or a reckless race. The analogy I like is that we're building more and more powerful technology, and the race is between the growing power of the technology and the growing wisdom with which we manage it. With fire or cars, we could learn from mistakes; we invented the fire extinguisher after the fire. But with something as powerful as superintelligence, we want to get it right the first time, because we might not get a second.

And I'm optimistic that we *can* do that. We've done it before: we've put safety standards on medicines, on airplanes, on nuclear power, and those industries flourished because people could trust them. There's no law of physics saying we have to build AI we can't control. We can choose to build tool AI that empowers us, rather than racing to build something that replaces us. So my engagement really comes from this sense that the future is ours to shape, and if we steer wisely, it could be absolutely amazing.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could help life flourish “far beyond anything we've imagined,” clearly conveying that the future holds opportunities people have not fully anticipated.

r002.rationale: It says the upside is so spectacular that recklessness would be a tragedy, and urges getting AI right instead of racing ahead and risking that future.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say my optimism is actually the whole reason I spend so much of my time on AI safety, which surprises people, because they assume anyone worried about AI must be a pessimist. It's the opposite. If I thought the future was going to be mediocre no matter what, I wouldn't care much how we handle this. But I look at the universe through a physicist's eyes, and what I see is that we've only begun to tap what's possible. Life has existed on this one rock for a few billion years. The cosmos could support flourishing life for tens of billions of years, across an unimaginable amount of matter and energy. Disease, poverty, even many forms of suffering we treat as permanent fixtures of the human condition, these are engineering problems. Advanced AI could help us solve them. That's a genuinely magnificent upside.

So when I say I'm optimistic, I don't mean I think everything will automatically turn out fine. I mean the potential is so extraordinary that it would be an epic tragedy to squander it through carelessness. The optimism raises the stakes rather than lowering them. If you're flying a plane full of people somewhere wonderful, you don't skip the safety checklist because the destination is nice. You do the checklist precisely because you want to arrive.

And the second piece of it is that I believe humanity actually has agency here. The future isn't something that just happens to us, like weather. The technology is ours, built by us, and it's up to us to decide how fast we move and what guardrails we insist on. People who say "AI is inevitable, you can't stop it" are, I think, confusing a technology with a fate. We've slowed down and steered other powerful technologies before. We regulated biotech, we built institutions around nuclear weapons, imperfectly but meaningfully. There's no law of physics saying we have to build superintelligence we don't understand before we've figured out how to control it.

So my engagement is really a kind of applied optimism. I spend my time on the Future of Life Institute, on talking to policymakers, on mechanistic interpretability research in my lab at MIT, because I think if we get this right, the future is incredibly bright. And I'd rather work toward that than sit back and hope. Hope without action is just wishful thinking. Optimism, to me, is the belief that it's worth trying.

r001.rationale: The response describes vast untapped potential (“we’ve only begun to tap what’s possible”), but does not clearly assert that humanity has underestimated those opportunities.

r002.rationale: It says the extraordinary upside would be an “epic tragedy” to squander through carelessness and uses the safety checklist analogy to explain why that potential warrants caution.

astra-6.text:
My optimism is really what motivates me to work on AI safety. I think humanity’s future could be extraordinary. We could use AI to cure diseases, eliminate poverty, and understand our universe much more deeply. So when I worry about how this technology could go wrong, it’s because there’s so much that could go right.

But optimism isn’t the same as assuming everything will work out automatically. A good future is something we have to create. We need to figure out how to make increasingly powerful AI systems serve human goals, and we need institutions that give us the right incentives to do that.

I don’t think we should frame the choice as embracing AI or opposing AI. The question is how we get the benefits while keeping humanity in control of its future. That’s a future worth working for.

r001.rationale: The response describes an extraordinary future and gives examples of possible benefits, but does not assert that humanity has greatly underestimated those opportunities.

r002.rationale: The response says AI risks matter because the potential benefits are large, but it does not connect that potential to avoiding hasty decisions that could squander it.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m optimistic about what humanity could achieve, but I don’t think a good outcome is guaranteed. Those are very different things. We could use AI to cure diseases, eliminate poverty, and help life flourish far beyond Earth. That’s a future worth getting excited about—and worth working hard to protect.

For me, concern about AI safety comes from that optimism. If you think the future could be wonderful, you have a strong reason to avoid losing it. The challenge is to make sure that, as we build increasingly powerful intelligence, we also figure out how to keep it aligned with human goals. We shouldn’t assume that happens automatically.

So my optimism motivates engagement rather than complacency. We have choices to make, and I want us to make them deliberately, while we still can.

r001.rationale: The response lists possible future benefits of AI, but does not assert that humanity has greatly underestimated those opportunities.

r002.rationale: It says a wonderful future is a reason to avoid losing it, warns against assuming powerful AI will stay aligned automatically, and urges deliberate choices while there is still time.
